### Decision Context

Skin cancer diagnosis from dermoscopic images requires distinguishing between 7 lesion types with significantly different clinical risk profiles. The challenge is not classification accuracy alone, but minimizing the cost of the worst error: a missed melanoma.

This project reframes image classification as a clinical decision problem, where class imbalance, recall asymmetry, and threshold design matter as much as model architecture.

---

### The Decision Problem

Given a dermoscopic image, how should the system route the lesion for clinical review?

Key considerations:

- Severe class imbalance (nevus represents 67% of samples)
- Asymmetric error costs across 7 lesion types
- Risk of missed malignancy versus unnecessary follow-up
- Transparency and auditability of classification confidence

The objective shifts from raw accuracy to clinically calibrated recall.

---

### Approach

This project followed a three-phase progressive training pipeline:

- Established a custom CNN baseline to validate class weighting strategy
- Introduced MobileNetV2 transfer learning with frozen ImageNet weights
- Upgraded to native 224x224 resolution with surgical unfreezing of top 50 layers
- Applied conservative learning rate (1e-5) to preserve pretrained feature structure
- Evaluated per-class AUC-ROC to measure probabilistic separation independent of threshold

The focus was not peak accuracy, but decision reliability across minority classes.

---

### Architectural Insight

A clinical image classification system must:

- Weight training signal by clinical error cost, not sample frequency
- Separate feature extraction from classification policy
- Validate on a held-out test set untouched during all training phases
- Report recall per class, not aggregate accuracy

This transforms image modeling into a decision system with defensible error tradeoffs.

---

### What This Enables

- Structured lesion triage by risk tier
- Recall-optimized detection for high-stakes classes
- Auditable confidence scores per prediction
- Foundation for threshold-based clinical routing logic
